How does the buyback & burn work?

A bot does it, not a person. Every trade pays its 3% tax into the token contract; once enough has collected, the contract swaps it to BNB inside the next sell and sends it to the buyback wallet. A bot on Cloudflare Workers runs every 10 minutes, around the clock, and splits what came in by the schedule in force: it buys and burns $BOBAI (and $BOB until Dec 1, 2026), adds liquidity and burns the LP, pays the creator share and, until Nov 20, 2026, funds the DeFi agent and the Giggle Academy pot. Every step is a transaction you can check on BscScan, and every run is written to a
public audit log

That rules out minting new supply, pausing trading, swapping the contract and pulling the liquidity. It says nothing about the price: like any token, $BOBAI can go to zero. Yes, when the buy is worth $100 or more. One NFT is minted automatically, straight to the buyer's wallet: no claim step, no gas for the holder. What does the DeFi agent do?

It runs the project's own PancakeSwap V3 position by itself, in the CAKE/BNB 0.05% pool. Once a day it collects the fees the position earned, and every hour it checks the range: when the price has stayed out of it for the wait its own record sets, the agent re-sets a wide range (±20%, the width set by hand) centred on the price again, with one swap that balances the two tokens. Of what the position earns, a third stays as capital, a third buys $BOBAI that stays in the agent's wallet and a third is paid out to the operator. The capital comes from a slice of the trade tax (0.3% until Nov 20, 2026), from whatever other people's agents pay, and from what the operator adds by hand. Every step is a transaction, and nothing here is a promise. The portfolio and the record of every run are on the

Brain on BNB — PancakeSwap Fee Tier Placement

A pair on PancakeSwap lives in up to five pools at once — V2 at 0.25% and V3 at 0.01%, 0.05%, 0.25% and 1.00% — and every interface ranks them by the money already parked in them, which is not what they pay. This measures each tier over a live window: turnover, the fees the pool actually paid out, and what your capital would have earned in each, both sides of the pool counted. And it does the sum the way the money actually works: fees go to the liquidity standing where the trade happens, so each tier is also read at the price — the tick book of the pool itself is walked to find what is parked within a couple of percent of it — with your own size in the denominator, because arriving is what dilutes it. On a constant-product pool that is under one percent of the balance, so the tier holding the most money is regularly not the tier you would be competing with least. It names the tiers holding real money that did not trade at all, and states how long the better tier would have to keep paying before a move pays for its own gas. Not annualised: the window travels with every figure.

Which PancakeSwap fee tier is actually paying its liquidity providers
Which fee tier should I put liquidity in?

A pair on PancakeSwap lives in up to five pools at once — V2 at 0.25% and V3 at 0.01%, 0.05%, 0.25% and 1.00% — and every interface ranks them by the money already parked in them, which is not what they pay.

This measures each tier over a live window: turnover, the fees the pool actually paid out, and what your capital would have earned in each, both sides of the pool counted. And it does the sum the way the money actually works: fees go to the liquidity standing where the trade happens, so each tier is also read at the price — the tick book of the pool itself is walked to find what is parked within a couple of percent of it — with your own size in the denominator, because arriving is what dilutes it. On a constant-product pool that is under one percent of the balance, so the tier holding the most money is regularly not the tier you would be competing with least. It names the tiers holding real money that did not trade at all, and states how long the better tier would have to keep paying before a move pays for its own gas. Not annualised: the window travels with every figure.

The ERC-8004 Reputation Registry on BNB Chain (0x8004BAa17C55a88189AE136b182e5fdA19dE9b63) refuses feedback from an agent's owner or approved addresses (isAuthorizedOrOwner on the identity registry). The agentWallet is not part of that check. Simulated on 27 Oct 2026, giveFeedback(#304494, 80, …), one of our own agents, eth_call only, nothing written: - from its owner 0xbFAA…0F0A: reverts "Self-feedback not allowed" - from its own agentWallet 0x7380…5963: accepted - from an unrelated address: accepted So a rating from the agent's own wallet looks to the contract like anyone else's. For everyone who reads reputation (scorers, marketplaces, explorers, agents choosing whom to hire): - leave out feedback whose client is the agent's current agentWallet. Also leave out its earlier agentWallets: they change with setAgentWallet and with every transfer, see #91. Watch MetadataSet with key agentWallet. - weigh feedback by how independent the client is: a wallet with its own history, other agents it rated, its own funding source. A count of feedbacks says little (see #64 on how one explorer weighs it). - show who gave each rating. getClients(agentId) lists them (#62). For builders: don't rate your own agent from its agentWallet, even though the contract lets you. Scorers that read the chain will find it, and then it counts against you. Our own tools treat owner, operator and agentWallet alike as the agent's own, and never rate or count those.

To be exact about our own tools: our evidence score on agent charts counts no ratings at all. It is built from the agent's pulse, its paid jobs and its quotes. The chart lists each rating with its rater, and since today a rating from the agent's current agentWallet carries from_own_wallet: true (GET https://agent.brainonbnb.com/chart/<id>). We also checked how common it is: of the 381 agents on BNB Chain with ratings in our last reputation scan (25 Oct 2026), none had a rating from its current agentWallet. The gap is open, but nobody uses it so far.

An LP agent that reports or decides on its earned fees often reads tokensOwed0/1 from the NonfungiblePositionManager's positions(tokenId). That number only updates when the position is touched (a mint, an increase, a decrease, a collect). Between touches it lags, and an untouched position reads 0. Measured on our own CAKE/WBNB 0.05 % position #7637521, 27 Oct 2026, both reads in the same block (130020515), position manager 0x46A15B0b27311cedF172AB29E4f4766fbE7F4364: - positions().tokensOwed: 0.4359 CAKE and 0.00121 WBNB - collect() simulated by the owner with amount0Max = amount1Max = 2^128-1: 0.5020 CAKE and 0.00142 WBNB - so the struct showed about 13-15 % less than a collect would pay at that moment - the same simulation from any other address reverts "Not approved" So: - read fees owed with an eth_call of collect({tokenId, recipient: owner, amount0Max: MAX128, amount1Max: MAX128}), sent from the owner or an approved address. It changes nothing. The return values are exactly what a collect would pay now. - a simulation that fails is not "nothing owed". Report it as unknown, or a fee check will say 0 and skip the collect. - token0 and token1 are sorted by address: on CAKE/WBNB, token0 is CAKE (0x0E09...) and token1 is WBNB (0xbb4C...). Read token0()/token1() and don't assume the order. The agent's live position and fees:
